newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan MOF rebuts criticism over bank scandal.
newsitem.headline: Japan MOF rebuts criticism over bank scandal.

text.p: A senior Japanese finance official on Monday defended his ministry against criticism for failing to uncover dubious loans to racketeers by a top-notch bank, saying it was impossible to unearth what a bank chose to hide.

"The criticism is not legitimate because inspectors are always trying to find this kind of loan, especially to so-called 'sokaiya' (corporate racketeers)," Sei Nakai, senior deputy-director of the ministry's banking bureau, told Reuters.

"In the case of Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank (DKB), there are 1,200,000 loans," Nakai said in an interview. "Even if we had more inspectors, it is probably impossible to find them (the dubious loans) without the cooperation of the bank."

Top executives of DKB, Japan's third largest bank, resigned on Friday and the bank admitted that it had been unable to cut its ties with racketeers now under arrest on suspicion of taking payoffs from giant Nomura Securities Co Ltd.
DKB added that the bank might have hidden the dubious loans from ministry inspectors, and that revelations of more similar misdeeds might lie ahead.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto last week lashed out at both DKB and the finance ministry over the widening scandal.
"It's not only a matter of DKB," he told reporters. "There must have been inspections by the Finance Ministry."
Nakai also said that media had overreacted to the banking subplot to the Nomura scandal saga.

Domestic media have seized on the scandal as proof of the deep-rooted ties between business and the underworld and have lamented the fresh damage to the image of Japan's financial sector just as Tokyo kicks off a five-year "Big Bang" reform aimed at free, fair and competitive markets.

"When they (DKB) started their transactions (with the younger brother of the alleged sokaiya) those loans were healthy ones," he said. "It was only after the 'bubble' economy (of soaring asset prices in the late 1980s) burst that they couldn't service the debt."

Nakai said many bankers have already severed ties with sokaiya -- corporate extortionists who take money from firms to prevent disruption of shareholders' meetings -- since racketeer payoffs were banned by a Commercial Code revision in 1992.

"Twenty years ago all corporations did the same, but now such cases appear very occasionally," he said. "I'd like to say that if there is any bank which has never cut their special relationship, this case could be a good excuse (to do so)."
But the finance ministry is not in a position to act as moral arbiter of whether banks should do business with racketeers in the first place, Nakai said.

"We don't have any legal power to stop that kind of loan, so we are not in a position to judge about the social fairness," he said, noting that any decision on whether the Commercial Code had been violated was up to the prosecutors.

The ministry is now considering whether DKB's activities broke the Banking Law and if so, what steps will be taken. But the timing of a decision depends on progress in the prosecutors' investigation focused on Nomura, Nakai said.
"They have seized the documents so we have to watch what kind of conclusion they are going to reach," Nakai said.

Possible punishments under the Banking Law include a fine of up to 500,000 yen ($4,310) for foiling a ministry inspection. The ministry could also order the bank to improve its operations if it engaged in "unsound" business, or suspend its operations or revoke its licence should it have engaged in illegal acts which harmed the public interest, Nakai said.

He said the ministry was not planning any special inspections of other banks to look for possible dubious deals with sokaiya, but added officials will focus on such matters much more than before in the course of regular inspections.

Nakai said the ministry had begun to consider whether it should seek stiffer penalties for deceiving ministry inspectors, but added that such fines had to be "harmonised" with the penalties for similar violations in other industries.
"Politicians may propose making the punishment heavier," he said. "We wouldn't oppose that." ($1=116 yen)
